groups.title: Silence in literature

questions.prompt: None of the following, if true, can be validly inferred from the passage EXCEPT:

options.text: The interpretation of silence in literature depends on the readers’ imagination rather than that of the writer.
The presence of silence in literature primarily indicates the breakdown or inadequacy of language as a communication system.
Non-verbal textual elements such as spacing and punctuation play a role in shaping meaning independently of spoken or written language.
Literary silence operates as an expressive strategy that can convey meanings which explicit language fails to adequately convey.

questions.prompt: On the basis of the passage, which one of the following best captures the paradox inherent in silence in literature?

options.text: Silence in literature reflects the absence of speech, yet often relies on linguistic context to become noticeable and acquire meaning.
Silence in literature eliminates verbal expression, yet enhances the emotional intensity experienced by readers.
Silence in literature emerges from the limitations of language, yet exceeds it in communication of meanings.
Silence in literature disrupts conventional communication, yet depends on structural elements of writing to produce meaning.

questions.prompt: What does the author most nearly mean by “absence” in the context of the passage?

options.text: Absence in literature primarily is a withholding of expression when language reaches its limits.
Absence in literature is as a literary device that generates meaning by influencing how language is interpreted.
Absence in literature is used to intensify emotional effects by reducing the density of verbal expression.
Absence in literature is the form of writing by drawing attention to non-verbal elements such as spacing and layout.

questions.prompt: The phrase “noise into a form of muteness” most nearly implies that:

options.text: When language becomes too much or confusing, it can stop making sense and end up working like silence.
When there is constant speech, it becomes hard for readers to notice pauses or silence in the text.
Using too many words shows that the writer can’t control their expression, which leads to a breakdown in communication.
Silence in literature can be created not just by leaving things unsaid, but also by twisting or distorting language.

groups.stimulus:
We usually think of literature as a world made of words. After all, stories are written, poems are spoken, and meaning seems to reside in language itself. But what if some of the most powerful moments in literature occur precisely when words fall away? Across modern writing, silence and absence are no longer treated as failures of expression. Instead, they function as meaningful forces in their own right, shaping how texts communicate what cannot easily be said.

Silence in literature is never simply emptiness. It only becomes noticeable when placed next to language—through gaps, pauses, omissions, or sudden restraint. As the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein famously observed, “What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence.” Yet this silence is not meaningless. On the contrary, it often signals the limits of language while pointing beyond them. What remains unspoken can evoke grief, trauma, desire, or ethical hesitation more powerfully than direct statement.

Modern writers have developed many ways of making silence visible on the page. Some strip language down to bare fragments or unfinished sentences. Others overwhelm the reader with excessive speech that collapses into incoherence, turning noise into a form of muteness. Still others rely on suggestion, metaphor, or irony—saying one thing while meaning another. These strategies allow authors to approach experiences that resist clear articulation, such as shock, loss, or social alienation. In such cases, silence becomes a mode of honesty rather than avoidance.

Absence also draws attention to the physical and visual qualities of writing. Blank spaces, punctuation marks, line breaks, and layout all shape meaning, even though they contain no words themselves. A pause created by an ellipsis or asudden white space on the page can alter rhythm, emotion, and interpretation. As literary theorists have noted, this emphasis on material form challenges the idea that writing merely records spoken language. Instead, it highlights writing as an independent expressive practice, capable of meaning through structure as much as through vocabulary.

Philosophically, silence forces us to rethink what language can and cannot do. Thinkers like Jacques Ranciére have argued that literature operates between the sayable, the conceivable, and the perceptible. Silence occupies this in-between zone. It does not abandon meaning; it reframes it. By withholding explicit explanation, literary silence invites readers into a more active role, asking them to sense, infer, and imagine rather than simply decode.

Silence also carries political weight. There is a crucial difference between silence that is chosen and silence that is imposed. Deliberate silence can suggest resistance, dignity, or moral refusal. Forced silence, on the other hand, often signals powerlessness or exclusion. Literary representations of speechlessness frequently dramatize this tension, revealing how voices are shaped—and sometimes erased—by social structures.

Ultimately, paying attention to silence and absence changes how we read. It reminds us that meaning does not reside only in what Is stated plainly. Sometimes, literature speaks most clearly when it pauses, falters, or leaves space behind. In those moments, silence is not the opposite of expression—it is one of its most profound forms.

questions.prompt:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Margaret Atwood argues that while we cannot always change reality, we can choose how we respond to it—and that choice can shape outcomes. She frames the world as both “half empty and half full”: on one side, environmental degradation, nuclear threats, inequality, and widespread despair; on the other, human awareness, technological capability, and democratic systems that make change possible. The dangers we face are not inevitable forces of nature but largely human-made problems, meaning they can also be prevented if there is enough collective will. Though the global situation may seem overwhelming, individuals are not powerless. Public opinion still influences political action, and meaningful change becomes possible when enough people demand it. Ultimately, Atwood's message is cautiously hopeful: by shifting our attitudes from apathy to engagement, we not only reinterpret reality but also participate in transforming it.

options.text: Margaret Atwood suggests that although we cannot control all circumstances, our chosen response—especially when shared collectively—can turn human-made crises into opportunities for meaningful change.
Margaret Atwood's central claim is that while reality may be daunting, it remains malleable because human-made problems can be reshaped through collective awareness and action.

Even in a world filled with serious human-made crises, Margaret Atwood argues that conscious, collective engagement—shaped by our choice of response—can transform both how we see reality and what we make of it.
Margaret Atwood argues that hope lies not in denying global crises but in recognizing that our responses—driven by awareness and will—can actively influence and improve outcomes.

groups.title: Complexity and economics

questions.prompt: All of the following statements are consistent with the author’s critique of equilibrium approaches in economics EXCEPT that:

options.text: Equilibrium frameworks explain economic patterns by identifying situations where, once an overall pattern appears, it remains stable as individual agents have no incentive to change their behavior.
The analytical elegance of equilibrium models comes partly from the fact that they rely on simplifying assumptions that deliberately leave out many processes that occur in real economies.

Because equilibrium approaches focus on patterns that would continue without any incentive for agents to change their behavior, they do not take account of innovation, experimentation, and structural change.
The principal limitation of equilibrium theory is that it ignores how aggregate outcomes influence individual behavior, even though such feedback is central to the functioning of real economies.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following statements correctly describes the relationship between the behaviour of individual agents and aggregate economic patterns?

options.text: Aggregate patterns in the economy emerge independently of individual behaviour and subsequently determine how agents act within markets.
Individual agents determine economic outcomes through their behaviour, but once aggregate patterns form they remain largely unaffected by those patterns.
Aggregate economic patterns emerge from the behaviour of individual agents and subsequently feed back to influence the behaviour of those very agents.
Aggregate patterns arise from the coordinated actions of agents whose behaviour is largely determined by stable equilibrium conditions.

questions.prompt: The author’s criticism of equilibrium-based economic models depends most crucially on which one of the following assumptions?

options.text: The real-world economy is too complex to be studied directly through the interaction of individual agents.
Economic theory must aim to identify stable conditions in which prices, strategies, and expectations remain mutually consistent across markets.
The primary strength of equilibrium models lies in their ability to provide mathematically elegant representations of economic relationships.
Stable conditions in real economies arise when the overall pattern is consistent with the behaviour of agents.

questions.prompt: Suppose economists observe that firms continuously modify strategies in response to emerging industry-wide patterns that themselves arise from earlier strategic choices. According to the passage, which one of the following approaches would be most appropriate for analysing such behaviour?

options.text: An approach that identifies the prices or strategies that would leave firms with no incentive to revise their behaviour.
An approach that examines how agents’ actions generate patterns which subsequently reshape those agents’ behaviour.
A rational approach that determines the expectations firms must possess for market outcomes to validate those expectations.
A mathematical framework that derives a stable configuration of prices and quantities consistent across all markets.

groups.stimulus:
The economy is a vast and complicated set of arrangements and actions wherein agents—consumers, firms, banks, investors, government agencies—buy and sell, speculate, trade, oversee, bring products into being, offer services, invest in companies, strategize, explore, forecast, compete, learn, innovate, and adapt. In modern parlance we would Say it is a massively parallel system of concurrent behavior. And from all this concurrent behavior markets form, prices form, trading arrangements form, institutions and industries form... and continually reshape the system.

One of the earliest insights of economics is that these aggregate patterns arise from individual behavior, and individual behavior in turn responds to these aggregate patterns. It is this recursive loop that connects with complexity. Complexity, in sciences, studies how elements form patterns and how those patterns feed back to alter them. Complexity is about formation —the formation of structures—and how this formation acts back upon the objects that bring it forth.

To look at the economy from a complexity viewpoint then means asking how it evolves. This requires examining in detail how individual agents’ behaviors together create some outcome and how this outcome in turn alters their behavior. Complexity asks how behaviors react to the pattern they together create, and how that pattern alters itself as a result. This is often a difficult question; we are asking how a process is generated from the purposed actions of many agents. And so economics early in its history took a simpler approach, more amenable to mathematical analysis. Instead of asking how agents’ behaviors would react to the aggregate patterns they caused, it asked what behaviors would be consistent with the aggregate patterns produced. It asked what patterns would call for no changes in micro-behavior and would therefore be in stasis, or equilibrium.

General equilibrium theory thus asked what prices and quantities would be consistent with—and pose no incentives for changing—the overall pattern of prices and quantities in the economy's markets. Classical game theory asked what strategies or allocations would be consistent with the best course of action for an agent, given the strategies his rivals might choose. Rational expectations economics asked what expectations would be validated by the outcomes these expectations together generated.

This equilibrium shortcut was a natural and even proper way to render patterns in the economy open to mathematical inquiry, and it achieved a great deal. Its central construct is not only mathematically elegant; it re-composes the economy in our minds, giving us a way to picture it in its wholeness. Yet there has been a price for this finesse. The neoclassical construction it fostered posits an idealized, rationalized world whose assumptions are often chosen for analytical convenience. It lives in a Platonic realm of order, stasis, and perfection, largely stripped of the ambiguous, the messy, the real.

If we assume equilibrium, we impose a strong filter: there is no scope for exploration, creation, adaptation, innovation, or structural change. Anything requiring adjustment must be sidelined or dropped from theory, leaving a beautiful but bloodless depiction. What if economics allowed the wider possibility and asked how agents in the economy might react to the very patterns they create? What would we see then?

questions.prompt:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Human progress can be understood through three major ways of learning about and controlling the world. The first involves recording and accumulating knowledge, allowing discoveries to persist and build over time. The second involves identifying general principles that explain how the world works, enabling prediction and application across contexts. However, many complex phenomena resist such simple, universal laws. A third approach has emerged that relies on large amounts of data and pattern recognition to make accurate predictions without necessarily offering clear explanations. This method enables effective control even in domains where understanding remains limited. While powerful, it carries risks, as its lack of transparency makes failures harder to anticipate. Together, these approaches represent distinct but evolving ways through which humans enhance their ability to predict, adapt to, and shape complex systems.

options.text: Human advancement rests on three distinct ways of learning—preserving knowledge, discovering universal laws, and use of large data-driven patterns— collectively improving our capacity to predict and shape complex systems, even as the last lacks understanding and carries new risks.

Human progress occurs through three ways of learning and controlling systems — building cumulative knowledge, formulating general laws, and using data-driven pattern recognition—each expanding our power, though the last operates without human understanding and hence carries the risk of failures that become harder to predict.

Human progress advances through three complementary learning modes— accumulating knowledge, deriving general laws, and using data-driven pattern recognition—each enhancing our ability to predict and control the world, though the last does so without transparency and with greater risk.

Human progress is driven by three different and mutually exclusive approaches— accumulating knowledge, discovering general laws, and exploiting data-driven patterns—each enhancing our ability to manage complex systems, even as the last prioritizes predictive success over failures and uncertainty over security.

groups.title: Genetic variation

questions.prompt: Which one of the following options best summarises the passage?

options.text: Recent advances in genome-wide screening have primarily demonstrated that mutations in “junk DNA” genes are the most significant contributors to disease, leading to promising therapeutic interventions such as gene editing.
The identification of thousands of genetic variants has made it possible to accurately predict complex traits and diseases, rendering biological interpretation of individual variants unnecessary.

The discovery of genetic variants outside genes has overturned earlier assumptions about “junk DNA,” revealing that numerous small-effect variants collectively influence traits and disease, though their interpretation and application remain contested.
The classification of most of the genome as “junk DNA” has been challenged mainly because some rare mutations in genes have been successfully linked to major diseases and drug development.

questions.prompt: The passage implies that the distinction between coding and non-coding DNA is:

options.text: irrelevant, as only mutations within coding regions have real importance for disease and treatment.
overstated, since non-coding regions once thought to be functionless can significantly influence traits and disease.
incorrect, because all regions of DNA are now believed to have clear biological functions.
irrelevant for research, since genetic research has stopped trying to separate coding and non-coding regions in genetic studies.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following conclusions is most consistent with the omnigenic theory mentioned in the passage?

options.text: Genes that are not directly linked to them may significantly influence complex traits.

questions.prompt: None of the following, if true, would weaken the author’s main argument EXCEPT:

options.text: Most complex traits can be accurately predicted using only a small set of variants located within coding regions of genes.
Many variants in non-coding regions have effects so small that they cannot be individually linked to specific biological mechanisms.
Increasing sample sizes in genetic studies continues to reveal ever larger numbers of variants associated with a given trait.
Some rare mutations within genes have been successfully identified as having strong effects on specific diseases.

groups.stimulus:
When it first became possible to screen the entire genome for common DNA sequence variants, some were discovered that contributed to disease, altered height and weight, and influenced other traits. Disconcertingly, very few turned out to be within genes. They were all found in parts of the genome whose function, if any, was unknown. Our genes make up only about 2 per cent of our DNA. Together with another 8 per cent or so of the genome, they encode important biological functions. The other 90 per cent is junk. It doesn’t do anything bad - the geneticist Sydney Brenner compared it to the stuff we keep, as opposed to the rubbish we throw away - but until recently there was no evidence that it did anything important either. In these genetic deserts, sequence variants could hardly be expected to matter.

It turns out that they do matter, not individually but in aggregate. A typical variant makes a miserably small contribution to disease risk, increasing it by 1 per cent or less above baseline (adding a millimetre to your height, say, or a gram to your weight). This makes them hard to find. Genetic studies with tens or hundreds of thousands of subjects are required. And there are many variants for each disease. In 2007, fifty risk variants were considered a lot, but as sample sizes for genetic studies increased, that number kept growing, first to hundreds then to thousands. One recent study of high blood pressure recruited a million people and found 2103 independent genetic signals. We still don’t know the full number: according to a recently proposed omnigenic theory, a given trait might be the product of variations affecting virtually every gene.

Some researchers are trying to work out what these sequence variants do, starting from the assumption that they somehow control the function of genes. Even if the effect of any individual variant on disease is small, linking it to a gene might lead to a drug target. This onerous path has made some progress, but it has been slow: almost twenty years after the first genetic studies of inflammatory bowel disease, the identification of the role of a sequence variant in a gene desert led to the creation of a new drug. Others have taken the position that the multitude of effects, and their small scale, makes biological interpretation of junk DNA meaningless, but that we can still gain information from it, for example by adding up the effects of all the variants carried by an individual in order to predict their disease risk. This approach is the premise of the screening tests that predict intelligence from a genetic analysis of embryos.

Some researchers have continued to seek the relatively rare but easier to study mutations within genes, to see if any of them cause (or prevent) disease. Finding mutations like this requires the sequencing of all twenty thousand genes in vast numbers of people. But the expense is worth it: mutations have been found in genes that affect the risk of obesity, liver disease, cholesterol levels and diabetes, and mutations in ten genes have been found that increase the risk for schizophrenia. Some genes are promising targets for editing: a clinical trial is currently underway that involves editing a gene to lower LDL cholesterol.

groups.title: Critical points and perturbations

questions.prompt: The passage suggests all of the following about the role of perturbations in complex systems EXCEPT that:

options.text: Small perturbations can help a system adjust or adapt if the system is already near a tipping point where it can react to changes around it.
Perturbations can be dangerous in noisy environments because the system might react strongly to random signals that actually don’t mean anything important.
Perturbations necessarily produce large-scale systemic transformations whenever a system approaches a critical point.
Small perturbations can actually keep a system stable by releasing pressure gradually, preventing bigger problems later.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following observations would most weaken the author’s claim that operating near critical points can be beneficial for adaptation?

options.text: Systems that operate close to critical points are significantly unstable and more likely to collapse in response to minor, inaccurate signals even when no conditions have changed.
In some biological systems, individuals are able to regulate how strongly the system responds to disturbances, thereby adjusting how close the system remains to a critical point.
Certain complex systems maintain stability by remaining far from critical points and adapt much more effectively through slow, incremental adjustments to environmental change.
When environmental conditions change rapidly, systems positioned near critical points can shift states quickly and adopt behaviours better suited to the new circumstances.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements would the author most likely agree with regarding climate-change tipping points?

options.text: Complex systems should always remain far from critical thresholds in order to avoid catastrophic transitions.
Systems undergoing environmental change will inevitably collapse once a critical threshold has been crossed.
Sensitivity to perturbations is uniformly beneficial whenever environments are uncertain or noisy.
Systems become vulnerable when their distance from critical points cannot be tuned and when disturbances may produce irreversible changes.

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph, the author claims that “when the world is moderately or very noisy—filled with random, uninformative events—sensitivity to perturbations is dangerous.” None of the following statements, if true, contradict this claim EXCEPT:

options.text: When systems function in environments full of random, uninformative disturbances, they can experience harmful changes if they react strongly to those perturbations.
Systems that are near critical points can benefit from reacting quickly to disturbances when those disturbances actually indicate real environmental change.
Systems that are very sensitive to perturbations often go through disruptive changes when they operate in environments where most signals are random or misleading.
Systems in environments full of random, uninformative disturbances will stay stable if they respond strongly and immediately to every perturbation.

groups.stimulus:
Stock market crashes are a bridge to another of nature's fascinating properties: the presence of tipping points or critical points, as they're called in physics. When a system ‘sits’ near a critical point, a small shock can cause a big shift. Sometimes, this means a shift into a new state - a group of fish shoaling (weakly aligned) detects a shark (the shock) and switches to a school formation (highly aligned), which is good for speedy swimming and confusing the predator. These tipping points are often presented in popular articles as something to avoid, for example, when it comes to climate change. But, in fact, as the shark example illustrates, sitting near a critical point can allow a system to adapt appropriately if the environment changes. As with timescale separation, tipping points can be useful design features - if distance from them can be modulated. For example, in a recent study of a large, captive monkey society it was found the social system was near a critical point such that a small rise in agitation - perhaps caused by a hot afternoon - could set off a cascade of aggression that would nudge the group from a peaceful state into one in which everyone is fighting. In this group there happened to be powerful individuals who policed conflict, breaking up fights impartially. By increasing or decreasing their frequency of intervention, these individuals could be tuning the group's sensitivity to perturbations - how far the aggression cascades travel - and thereby tuning distance from the critical point.

We still don’t know how widespread this sort of tuning is in biological systems. But like degree of timescale separation, it’s something we can build into human systems to make them more fluid and adaptive - and therefore better able to respond to volatility and shocks. In the case of healthcare, that might mean having the financial and technological capacity to build and dismantle temporary treatment facilities at a moment’s notice, perhaps using 3D-printed equipment and biodegradable or reusable materials. In the economy, market corrections that burst bubbles before they get too large serve this function to some extent - they dissipate energy that has built up within the system, but keep the cascade small enough that the market isn't forced into a crash.

Climate-change activists warning about tipping points are right to worry. Problems arise when the distance from the critical point can't be tuned, when individuals make errors (such as incorrectly thinking a shark is present), and when there’s no resilience in the system - that is, no way back to an adaptive state after a system has been disturbed. Irreversible perturbations can lead to complete reconfigurations or total system failure. Reconfiguration might be necessary if the environment has changed, but it will likely involve a costly transition, in that the system will need time and resources to find satisfactory solutions to the new environment.

When the world is moderately or very noisy - filled with random, uninformative events - sensitivity to perturbations is dangerous. But it’s useful when a strategic shift is warranted (eg, a predator appears) or when the environment is fundamentally changing and the old tactics simply won't do. Understanding when to stay far from critical points, when to sit near them, and how to tune distance from them is central to designing adaptive, resilient systems.

groups.stimulus: An algorithmic trading simulation tracked exactly four stocks Stock W, Stock X, Stock Y, and Stock Z over a four-day trading week (Day 1 to Day 4). Every single day from Day 2 to Day 4, exactly four price-change events occurred in the closing prices of each of the four stocks w.r.t the closing price the previous day, as shown below: 1. Exactly one stock hit the Upper Circuit (i.e. its closing price was higher by ₹50 w.r.t the previous day's closing price). 2.
